Last night, Uncle Joe was blind drunk but this morning he is as.......as a judge
25395.explanation:
The word "drunk" refers to a state of intoxication due to alcohol consumption. The opposite of being drunk is being sober, meaning not under the influence of alcohol. The word that best conveys the opposite meaning of "drunk" and fits the gap is "sober."

So, the corrected sentence reads: "Last night, Uncle Joe was blind drunk, but this morning he is as sober as a judge." It contrasts the intoxicated state from the previous night with the clear-headed and not under-the-influence state in the morning.

"About" can also be used but it is less formal and not as precise as "on" If you make use of "about", you might not be suggesting that the central topic in the research is the "students' riot" but, there is a little bit of information about it in the report. 25436.explanation:
"Joel is one of those fanatical sports fans who talk about nothing else."

Sometimes, when who, that, whose and which is used, confusion about the choice of appropriate verbs sets in. The law of concord provides that who will refer to the noun or pronoun that comes before it and that noun or pronoun must become the subject. In the sentence above, who refers to the "fanatical sports fans" which is now the subject and it attracts the plural verb "talk" (plural of talks). But this does not change the fact that "Joel talks about nothing else", however, Joel is one of those "fanatical sports fans who talk about nothing else."

25439.question_text:
From the words or group of words lettered A to D, choose the word or group of words that best completes each of the following sentences.
No sooner............it started to rain
25439.explanation:
"No sooner...than" is the appropriate correlative conjunction. This means that whenever you use "no sooner", the appropriate conjunction is "than". 

The complete sentence would be: "No sooner had he arrived home than it started to rain."

The conjunction is used to indicate that one event happens immediately after another. In this case, the sentence means that as soon as he arrived home, it started to rain.

25441.explanation:
The phrase "scarcely had [subject] [past participle] when [event]" is a common grammatical structure used to indicate that one event happened immediately after another. 

In this sentence, "Scarcely had I opened the door when the dog came running in," the word "scarcely" implies that hardly any time passed between opening the door and the dog running in. The correct conjunction to use in this structure is "when."

25442.explanation:
The phrase "heads of state" is the plural form of "head of state." In this context, you are referring to multiple individuals who hold the position of head of state. The word "heads" is the plural form of "head," and "of state" remains unchanged in the plural form.

So, the completed sentence is: "Several heads of state attended the two-day summit." This implies that multiple leaders or individuals holding the position of head of state were present at the summit.

25444.subject: English Language
25444.question_text:
From the words or group of words lettered A to D, choose the word or group of words that best completes each of the following sentences.
I saw him again........last week
25444.explanation:
The difference between "some time" and "sometime" lies in their usage and meaning:

  • Some time: This is a two-word phrase where "some" acts as an adjective describing "time." It refers to a certain period or span of time, often implying a long duration. For example, "It will take some time to finish the project."

  • Sometime: This is a single word that functions as an adverb. It refers to an unspecified point in time, either in the past or future. For example, "Let's meet sometime next week."

Now, for the sentence "I saw him again........last week," the correct answer is D. sometime. The phrase "sometime" fits best because it indicates an unspecified period during the last week.

25455.explanation:
Verb

 Infinitive Definition Present Past Past Participle

Present Participle

lay

 to lay something down to put or place lay(s) laid laid

laying

lie 

 to lie to rest or recline lie(s) lay lain

lying

Illustration: 

  1. Using "lay" (to lay something down):

    • Present: She lays the book on the table every evening.
    • Past: Yesterday, she laid the flowers on the grave.
    • Past Participle: She has laid out all the materials for the project.
    • Present Participle: She is laying the foundation for a new building.

  2. Using "lie" (to rest or recline):

    • Present: The cat lies in the sunbeam for hours.
    • Past: Yesterday, the dog lay on the sofa all day.
    • Past Participle: The blanket had lain untouched for days.
    • Present Participle: The patient is lying in bed recovering from surgery.

"Won't" is more about future actions and does not fit well in this context, especially with the use of the word "rather" in the sentence which suggests that the speaker is trying to make a suggestion rather than talk about future actions.
